newsitem.title: FRANCE: GAN's rescue latest in string of French bailouts.
newsitem.headline: GAN's rescue latest in string of French bailouts.

text.p: The rescue of French insurer GAN is the latest in a string of costly government bailouts to prepare publicly owned firms for privatisation and end a tradition of state domination of the economy.

The government is expected to pump up to 20 billion francs into GAN to cover big provisions for real estate losses, mainly at its UIC unit which lent its way through the 1980s boom, only to come to grief when the property bubble burst.

That sum pales besides the 100 billion francs or more Credit Lyonnais, once Europe's biggest bank, is likely to cost taxpayers as a result of a mix of the property slump, reckless lending and a deep recession.
But it underscores the perils facing Prime Minister Alain Juppe's administration this year as it seeks not to strain public finances in preparing for European monetary union.
France is pledged to reduce public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 in order to qualify for membership in the planned single currency.
It also focuses the spotlight on how much France's property downturn which began in mid-1990 has cost taxpayers through the exposure of state-run lending institutions to real estate.

On top of the property woes of Credit Lyonnais and GAN, last year the European Union approved 15.2 billion in state aid to real estate lender Comptoir des Entrpreneurs. And the government plans a 2.6 billion franc wind-down of property lender Credit Foncier de France.

The cost of funding defeasance structures set up to hold their nonperforming property assets has run into billions of francs. About the only good news for taxpayers is that U.S. vulture funds have begun to circle the distressed property market and may take some of holdings off their hands.
France has been selling off state firms since 1986 but most of its biggest -- and most lucrative -- privatisations are behind it with the exception of France Telecom.
The sale of a first tranche of France Telecom in May is targeted to provide nearly all the 27 billion francs in privatisation revenues expected this year.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis promised last November all the 1997 privatisation money would be used for capital injections into state companies. "Never has there been such a big effort to help public enterprises," he said.
Credit Lyonnais is slated to get up to a 15 billion franc recapitalisation this year, on top of 45 billion francs in aid received in 1995, to knock it into shape for sale in 1999.
The latest sum will not include the up to 20 billion franc cost of softening a loan the bank made under the 1995 state bailout to finance spinoff of dud assets from its balance sheet.
Other firms in line for help this year are money-losing consumer electronics firm Thomson Multimedia, whose planned sale to Korea's Daewoo was aborted last year after strong opposition.

The government has refused to say whether Thomson Multimedia will get as much as the 10 billion francs it was slated to receive under the cancelled sell-off. Air France, due to be privatised in a year, has already got 20 billion francs.

Other beneficiaries of public largesse will include coal mining interests and a new state-owned holding firm being set up to assume some of the railway system's debt and take over ownership of France's railway infrastructure.
